statement: Intraspecific scaling of maximum dioxygen use changes with developmental stage.

scores.rationale: The stylized fact states that intraspecific oxygen-use scaling changes with developmental stage. Numerous snippets (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10, 11, 13, 16) explicitly state the canonical DEB respiration stylized fact: oxygen use increases with DECREASING mass in embryos but increases WITH mass in juveniles and adults — a direct qualitative reversal of the scaling relationship across developmental stages, exactly the pattern claimed. Snippet 1 adds mechanistic explanation (reserve loss in embryos vs. structure-driven maintenance in juveniles/adults; weight-specific O2 use declining over the life cycle). Snippet 12 supports the general notion that the metabolic-rate trajectory varies over the life cycle. Several snippets are listed citations (multiple references), reinforcing empirical grounding. Off-topic or only tangential items (8, 14, 15, 17, 18) do not contradict the fact. There is no contradicting evidence in the corpus, yielding strong, multiply-corroborated support.

scores.rationale: Two snippets directly bear on the stylized fact. Snippet [7] explicitly measures metabolic allometry/oxygen consumption across developmental stages in Bombyx mori and notes scaling coefficients differing across stages, strongly supporting that the scaling of dioxygen use changes with developmental stage. Snippet [10] shows respiration (ETS) rates differing by developmental stage in fish larvae versus juveniles, also consistent. The remaining snippets concern oxygen as a developmental morphogen, hypoxia effects on embryos, redox biology, dioxin toxicity, or epigenetics, and do not address intraspecific scaling of maximum oxygen use across ontogeny. Thus evidence is moderate (mainly one strong and one supporting reference) and what evidence exists points in the supporting direction with no contradiction.

Empirical studies (19, 22) independently document stage-dependent metabolic scaling and developmental-stage differences in respiration rate in silkworm and fish, corroborating the pattern. The remaining snippets concern oxygen/redox effects on development or unrelated topics and are neutral. No snippet contradicts the fact, so the evidence is strong and consistent.

snippets.text: ABSTRACT Deoxygenation, the reduction of oxygen level in the oceans induced by global warming and anthropogenic disturbances, is a major threat to marine life. This change in oxygen level could be especially harmful to marine embryos that use endogenous hypoxia and redox gradients as morphogens during normal development.

snippets.title: Environmental Oxygen is a Key Modulator of Development and Evolution: From Molecules to Ecology
snippets.label: neutral
snippets.text: Abstract Oxygen is a key regulator of both development and homeostasis and a promising candidate to bridge the influence of the environment and the evolution of new traits. To clarify the various ways in which oxygen may modulate embryogenesis, its effects are reviewed at distinct organizational levels. First, the role of pathways that sense dioxygen levels and reactive oxygen species are reviewed.
